questions.q: Why does flipping MFA enforcement for an entire organization at once usually fail?
options: MFA systems technically cannot support more than a few hundred users at a time
It always improves security with no operational downside
It locks out unenrolled users, shared-device users, and legacy-app users all at once, overwhelming support and often getting the policy reverted
It is illegal to enforce MFA for all users simultaneously
questions.explain: A single all-at-once enforcement concentrates every edge case into one spike instead of staging the risk across phases.

questions.q: In a phased MFA rollout, why are high-privilege accounts typically enrolled early despite pushing back the hardest?
options: Because privileged users never object to new security requirements
Because privileged accounts are technically unable to use MFA later in the rollout
Because general staff accounts are always more valuable targets
Because they are the accounts attackers want most, so protecting them early shrinks the real window of exposure
questions.explain: Admin and privileged accounts are high-value targets, so the rollout protects them early even though they're often the most resistant group.

questions.q: What is a break-glass account, and how should it be handled in an MFA rollout?
options: An emergency-access credential deliberately excluded from normal MFA enforcement, but tightly monitored with alerts on any use
An account that is deleted immediately once MFA is enabled org-wide
A shared account used by the entire IT department for daily work
A regular user account that happens to have a weak password
questions.explain: Break-glass accounts exist so admins aren't locked out during an identity-provider outage, but they must be few, monitored, and alerted on any sign-in.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how should a legacy application with no MFA support typically be handled?
options: Ignored, since legacy apps are not a real concern for MFA rollouts
Given a deliberate, documented, time-bounded exception, or placed behind a layer that adds MFA, or scheduled for replacement
Forced to support MFA overnight with no exception process
Immediately shut down with no transition plan
questions.explain: Legacy apps that can't support MFA need an explicit, tracked exception rather than being silently left out or forced to comply instantly.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat user communication and help-desk staffing as real engineering work for an MFA rollout?
options: Because users never have questions about enrolling a second factor
Because communication has no measurable effect on rollout success
Because help-desk staffing only matters after the rollout is fully complete
Because ticket volume reliably spikes each time a new phase goes live, and skipping preparation is where rollouts actually fail
questions.explain: Clear advance communication and staffed support during each phase's launch window are part of the rollout's design, not an afterthought.
